title: Brand positioning and messaging
summary: Decide who you serve, what you solve and why someone should choose you.
why: Clear positioning keeps websites, ads and sales conversations consistent.
Evidence makes a claim specific and credible.
know: Prioritize audiences and situations, then define the category, difference, evidence and main action.
Build messages around a core claim, supporting reasons, proof and buying-stage needs.
Give examples of tone. Adapt Chinese and English copy to their markets while keeping product facts consistent.
inputs: Interviews, customer research and existing brand assets
Competitors, markets, product facts and publishable evidence
Target markets, prohibited claims and reviewer
actions: Compare audience problems and competitor claims. Separate facts, assumptions and interview questions.
Propose positioning options and tradeoffs, with website, ad and sales examples.
Deliver a one-page positioning brief, message hierarchy, tone guide and bilingual glossary.
done: Claims have evidence; customer stories, numbers and certifications are accurate.
Messages share a position and offer the audience a suitable next step.
pitfalls: Treating translation as a market strategy.
decision: Agree on positioning, primary messages and public commitments.

reader.concept: Positioning explains who you serve, what you solve and why people should choose you. Messaging makes those answers easy to understand.
reader.when: Use this for a new brand, homepage redesign or inconsistent team messaging.

example.situation: A homepage promises low prices, premium quality, speed and customization at once.
example.lesson: Choose the main audience and promise, then support it with facts.

reader.first_step: Write down your primary audience and their strongest reason to choose you.

diagram.title: How a message takes shape
diagram.caption: Use the same core message across the website, presentations and ads.
